posts.author: Alan Sailer
posts.content_md:
I was saving my last few photopolymer plates to try and make a single beam transmission hologram using a 

mirror so that the objects can be more sidelit.

I had what I thought was a good diagram showing how to do this but when I went to try out the set-up it made 

no sense. I have found diagrams that make more sense but the common thread is that you need to expand 

the beam a LOT more than for a single beam densiyuk.

I am afraid that making a single beam with a mirror will require hours of exposure time. I already have to use 

half hour exposures with the denisyuk set-up. My green laser is 25mW and my plates are 10cm square.

Any advice?

Cheers.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
There is a thread on this forum called "Single beam transmission" which is from 2013. If you haven't seen it, use the search function for "Single beam transmission" (with quotes) to find it.

I've never done one myself, but they used to teach this method at the Fine Arts Research and Holographic Center (and Museum of Holography) at 1134 West Washington in Chicago (now defunct). I've attached a link to a page from the notes they provided when I attended. I don't think there is a real need to expand the beam substantially, it's just that the more you expand it, the bigger the scene becomes. The objects will be back-lit using this method. There is also a second SBT method they described as "division of amplitude" which uses a mirror (maybe this is what you had in mind), and the object is front-lit.

[https://www.holographyforum.org/forum/d ... &mode=view](https://www.holographyforum.org/forum/download/file.php?id=2391&mode=view)

posts.author: Alan Sailer
posts.content_md:
Joe,

Thank you very much. Like I said, none of the other diagrams I saw made sense until you linked me to one that did.

I have made two transmission holograms that came out fine. The wide exposure latitude of the GEOLA film really helps.

I am wondering what the advantages of single beam (SB) transmission are over SB reflection. My observations so far;

1) The viewing angle for transmission holograms is amazing.

2) There is lots of speckle due to the need to use a laser to view the hologram.

3) You need a laser to view the hologram.

4) The lighting appears more natural compared to a reflection Denisyuk.

The books I have don't really describe very well what the advantages/disadvantages of various hologram types are. 

Overall I'm more impressed by reflection holograms.

Cheers.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: Glad it worked. It seems that every type of hologram has its own set of qualities. I guess it depends on what you like, or what you're interested in. The same with the recording material. Nowadays, it's very difficult to see a variety of holograms in person. I was lucky to be within an hour's drive of the Chicago Museum of Holography, which I visited frequently from the beginning of the 80's (maybe late 70's, I can't remember) until it closed some years ago. I might suggest building a small collection of different types of holograms. Ebay is ideal for this, and it shouldn't be too expensive. As for books, there are many, but my favorite is the second edition of Practical Holography by Graham Saxby. For your own experiments, the Bayfol material should be ideal.

posts.author: Alan Sailer
posts.content_md:
Yes. Seeing stuff like this in person is always best.

This whole boondoggle started after my wife and I visited the Getty Center exhibit on holography. It was by far the best display of holograms I've seen. They don't tell you technical details because...art museum.

AS we left the exhibit I asked her if she wanted me to try out holography. Sure she said. I found out that all the holo kit makers are having issues so I bought a used LitiHolo kit from ebay. Like an idiot I never thought about ageing film so that was a bust. the next step was buying from Geola.

Once again, I feel lucky for all the help I've gotten from this forum. I always feel weird asking questions that I am sure have been asked and answered many times before. And I'm sure this help is why all my first holograms have been very nice. In fact, I've only had about three exposures that I consider failures.

Cheers.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
If you're in the Phoenix area, visit my exhibit "Vintage Lasers & Holograms" in Tempe. You'll see many of the different types of holograms, and I can bring more in for your visit. The focus of my personal holography these days is on making large transmission holograms in photopolymer film. 

You may also want to visit Kendall's Kitchen in Pacific Beach (near San Diego) to see Peter Scheir's newly opened exhibit of holograms from his large collection. My 8x10" transmission hologram "Grandma's Tea Set" in on display there.
